input.said: What does Seth use the Antikythera mechanism to show?

cases.reply:
He uses it as an example of an early computer that was analogue, not digital. It is a historical illustration, and it is not a proof. He says the earliest computers were not digital Turing machines but analogue devices operating in continuous time [spya-zg9me8]. That claim sits inside his second argument, "Other Games In Town". The argument is that Turing-style computation is only one kind, and that other kinds of dynamics and function lie beyond it [spya-gw0hsq]. The mechanism is the oldest case in a short history that continues with 1950s cybernetics and then neuromorphic and "mortal" computation [spya-zg9me8 spya-kjfjgm]. That history sets up his claim that these alternatives are less substrate-flexible than digital computation [spya-kjfjgm].

One detail in the passage looks wrong. The article dates the mechanism to "around 2,000 BCE" [spya-zg9me8]. Sources I found give a date about 2,000 years ago. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antikythera_mechanism) lists it as made in the 2nd century BC, and the [World History Encyclopedia](https://www.worldhistory.org/Antikythera_Mechanism/) dates it to roughly 205–60 BCE. My inference is that "2,000 BCE" is a slip for "2,000 years ago". It doesn't affect his point.

input.said: What does Seth say about Chalmers' neural replacement thought experiment?

cases.reply:
Seth says the thought experiment fails at the start, because its key premise can't be met. The argument asks us to imagine replacing brain parts one at a time with silicon parts that work in exactly the same way, and to conclude that consciousness doesn't depend on the material. He says it "fails at its first hurdle," since no part of the brain can be swapped for a perfect silicon equivalent [spya-ahtr6e]. He also notes that Hinton recently used it to claim conscious AI is already here [spya-ahtr6e].

His reason comes just before this. Real brains are tightly integrated across scales, so you can't assume one neuron can be replaced by a silicon version that keeps its input-output behavior exactly the same [spya-jnwfxp]. His example is work by Chintaluri and Vogels, who found that some neurons fire to clear metabolic waste. Replacing those would mean building a silicon metabolism too, and he says silicon isn't suited to that [spya-un9fjn]. His conclusion is that the only perfect replacement for a biological neuron is another biological neuron [spya-un9fjn].

My inference is that this fits his broader aim. The thought experiment assumes the substrate (the physical material) doesn't matter, which is the point he is contesting in this section. His case that brains can't cleanly separate what they do from what they are [spya-zw2m7u] would make that assumption look circular.

The article doesn't say how Chalmers or others have answered this objection. If you want that, I can search for it.
